name: Balaam
bio:
Balaam was the son of Beor, living at Pethor near the Euphrates — a pagan prophet of renown among the nations, believed able to bless or curse at will. When Balak, king of Moab, grew terrified of Israel, he hired Balaam at great cost to curse them, making Balaam's story one of the most strange and dramatic episodes in the Bible.

## 👤 Identity and Background: A Hired Pagan Prophet

Balaam at first refused Balak's invitation because God told him, "Do not curse these people, for they are blessed." But when Balak sent even more distinguished messengers with a greater reward, God allowed Balaam to go, on the condition that he speak only what God commanded him (Numbers 22:1-20).

## 📖 Core Story: The Talking Donkey and the Prophecies of Blessing

1. **The Donkey Sees the Angel of the LORD Three Times**: As Balaam rode his donkey, the angel of the LORD stood in the road with a drawn sword to block him; the donkey saw the angel three times and swerved away, but Balaam could not see it and struck the donkey three times in anger. Then the LORD opened the donkey's mouth, and it rebuked Balaam for beating it; only then were Balaam's eyes opened to see the angel standing in the road, who warned him to speak only what God commanded (Numbers 22:21-35).
2. **Three Altars, Three Blessings**: Balak built altars and offered sacrifices three times, hoping Balaam would curse Israel, but each time Balaam opened his mouth, his words became blessing instead of cursing, declaring, "God is not a man, that he should lie, nor a son of man, that he should change his mind... I have received a command to bless; he has blessed, and I cannot change it" (Numbers 23:19-20).
3. **The Messianic Prophecy**: In his fourth oracle, Balaam delivered one of the most important messianic prophecies in Scripture: "A star will come out of Jacob; a scepter will rise out of Israel... [who] will crush the foreheads of Moab, [and] crush all the people of Sheth" (Numbers 24:17) — a prophecy later understood to foreshadow the Davidic dynasty and ultimately the coming of Jesus Christ.

## ✨ Key Character and Theological Significance

- **A Prophet Used by God Despite His Own Heart**: Though Balaam coveted Balak's reward and likely did not truly fear the LORD, God still used his mouth to speak pure blessing and prophecy, showing that God governs all things — even the speech of a pagan diviner is subject to his authority.
- **A Warning Against Greed and Apostasy**: Despite the blessings he pronounced, Balaam later devised a plan to lure Israel into sexual immorality with Moabite women and the worship of Baal of Peor (Numbers 25; 31:16), and the New Testament repeatedly invokes "Balaam's error" and "the wages of Balaam" as warnings against false teachers who seek unrighteous gain through religious authority (2 Peter 2:15; Jude 11; Revelation 2:14).

Balaam's story reminds us that God's word and purpose cannot be bent by human malice — even a deceitful, mercenary man's own mouth, when speaking what God has commanded, will fulfill it to the letter. Later, when Israel was sent to avenge the evil of Baal Peor against the Midianites, Balaam himself was killed by the sword in that battle, bringing his greedy, apostate life to its end (Numbers 31:8). 2 Peter later cites him as a cautionary example of greed for unrighteous wages, referring to him there as "the son of Bosor" rather than Beor — likely a textual or dialectal variant rather than a different figure (2 Peter 2:15).
